## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sekha Sutta* ("A Trainee", MN 53; PTS MN i 353) is the fifty-third discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Set at the newly built assembly hall (*santhāgāra*) of the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu, the Buddha is invited to inaugurate the building with a sermon [SuttaCentral; Freedman 1977; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. After addressing the Sakyans late into the night, the Buddha suffers from back pain and requests Venerable Ānanda to deliver an exposition on the trainee's path of practice (*sekha-paṭipadā*) while he rests [Freedman 1977; Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra; Galasek 2016]. A *sekha* ("trainee" or "learner") denotes a noble disciple who has entered any of the three lower planes of sanctity (stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning) but must still continue training toward final liberation (*arahantship*) [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

Ānanda outlines the trainee's progress through fifteen factors of conduct (*caraṇa*), consisting of eleven preliminary qualities followed by the four *jhāna*s [Freedman 1977; Rogell 2003]. The preliminary course involves ethical discipline (*sīla*), restraint of the senses, moderation in eating, wakefulness, and seven noble qualities (*saddhamma*): faith, moral shame, moral dread, learning, energetic effort, mindfulness, and wisdom discerning rise and fall [Freedman 1977; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism]. Grounded in this conduct, the disciple attains the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), reaching in the fourth *jhāna* an unsurpassable purity of equanimity and mindfulness [Davis & Flanagan, Mirror is for Reflection; Anālayo 2003]. This meditative mastery leads to the three true knowledges (*tevijjā*): recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) [Davis & Flanagan, Mirror is for Reflection; Rogell 2003]. Buddhaghosa provides an extensive commentary on the sutta in the *Papañcasūdanī* [McTighe, Mentoring in the Majjhima Nikaya].
While the *Sekha Sutta* lacks a direct parallel in the extant Chinese Āgamas, a version of it is cited in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (*Dazhidulun*) [Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. SuttaCentral identifies numerous thematic parallels sharing the sequential formulas of gradual training, sense restraint, and the *jhāna*s (such as DN 2, DN 33, MN 27, MN 39, MN 107, and SN 35.120) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus documents substantial Pali-internal text reuse with several *Aṅguttara Nikāya* chapters (AN 3, AN 4, AN 5, AN 7, AN 8, AN 10, AN 11), SN 35, and the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), which shares the framing narrative of an assembly hall's opening [DharmaNexus; Freedman 1977]. DharmaNexus also aligns the sutta with cross-language parallels in the Sanskrit *Saṅgītisūtra*, the *Daśabalasūtra*, and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* in Sanskrit and Tibetan [DharmaNexus].
